𝗜𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗦𝗖𝗗 𝗧𝗬𝗣𝗘 𝟭 𝗜𝗡 𝗣𝗬𝗦𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗞: 𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗪𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗘 𝗖𝗨𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗠𝗘𝗥 𝗗𝗔𝗧𝗔 𝗪𝗜𝗧𝗛𝗢𝗨𝗧 𝗛𝗜𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗬

Ever needed to refresh your customer records without cluttering your database with past versions? Let’s explore a straightforward PySpark approach to implement SCD Type 1 and keep your data up to date—no history tracking required.

𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝗖𝗗 𝗧𝘆𝗽𝗲 𝟭 
SCD (Slowly Changing Dimension) Type 1 is all about overwriting outdated dimension data with new values. Unlike Type 2, there’s no versioning—think of it as updating your LinkedIn headline: the previous title is gone once you save the change.

𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗼:
Imagine your marketing team delivers a daily JSON dump of customer profiles (`customer_id`, `email`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `signup_date`). Updates come through as corrected typos or new email addresses. How do you ensure your master table always reflects the latest truth?

𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝘆𝗦𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝗝𝗼𝗯 

𝟭.𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗮 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘁 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮 
 Enforce data types from the start to catch bad records before they crash the job.

𝟮.𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻-𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰 - 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗖𝗗 𝗧𝘆𝗽𝗲 𝟭

 𝗜𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻 : Identify existing customers whose records need updating.
 𝗟𝗲𝗳𝘁 𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻 : Retain customers not present in today’s feed (no change).
 𝗟𝗲𝗳𝘁 𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗶-𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻 : Detect brand-new customers for insertion.

𝟯. 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗻 
 Combine updated rows, untouched rows, and new inserts into a single DataFrame that represents the current state.

𝟰. 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗖𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 
 Since the existing customer table is joined three times, caching it avoids repetitive reads and speeds up processing.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 

𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 : No historical baggage slowing down queries.
𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 : Always query the one “current” version.
𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 : Direct overwrites are more efficient than versioning.

existing_customers_data =
 [ (1001, "john.doe@email.com", "John", "Doe",datetime.date(2024, 1, 15) ,datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 0, 0) # datetime object ),
 (1002, "jane.smith@email.com", "Jane", "Smith",datetime.date(2024, 2, 20), datetime.datetime(2024, 2, 20, 11, 30, 0) ),
 (1005, "charlie.davis@email.com", "Charlie", "Davis",datetime.date(2024, 1, 1),datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 1, 9, 15, 0))]

daily_updates_data = 
[(1001, "john.doe.updated@email.com", "John", "Doe", "2024-01-15"), 
 (1002, "jane.smith@email.com", "Jane", "Smith-Johnson", "2024-02-20"), 
 (1003, "bob.wilson@email.com", "Robert", "Wilson", "2024-03-10"), 
 (1004, "alice.brown@email.com", "Alice", "Brown", "2024-04-05") ]

ai_analysis.summary: The post outlines a PySpark approach for maintaining a customer master table with Slowly Changing Dimension Type 1. A daily JSON feed contains customer profiles and may include corrected values, changed email addresses, and new customers. The proposed process identifies updated records with an inner join, unchanged records and new customers with left anti-joins, unions the three groups into the current state, and overwrites the existing customer data without preserving history. It recommends defining an explicit schema and caching the existing customer table because that table is joined three times. The provided content includes sample existing and daily-update data, but it does not include a complete executable PySpark transformation or write job.
subtopics: Separating updated, unchanged, and new customer records

interview_questions.question: What distinguishes SCD Type 1 from a dimension strategy that preserves previous versions?
interview_questions.answer:
SCD Type 1 overwrites outdated dimension values with the latest values.
SCD Type 1 does not retain historical versions of the overwritten values.
The stated benefits are simpler current-state queries and more efficient storage than versioning.

interview_questions.question: How can joins and anti-joins separate a daily customer feed into updated, unchanged, and new records?
interview_questions.answer:
An inner join identifies existing customers whose records appear in the daily feed and require updates.
A left anti-join from the existing table to the daily feed retains existing customers absent from the feed.
A left anti-join from the daily feed to the existing table identifies new customers that require insertion.

interview_questions.question: Why does the proposed process cache the existing customer table?
interview_questions.answer:
The existing customer table participates in three joins.
Caching is intended to avoid repetitive reads and speed up processing.

interview_questions.question: Why should an explicit schema be defined before processing the customer feed?
interview_questions.answer:
Defining data types from the start helps enforce input consistency.
Schema enforcement can catch bad records before they crash the job.

interview_questions.question: How should the final customer master DataFrame be assembled under the described SCD Type 1 process?
interview_questions.answer:
The final DataFrame should combine updated existing records, unchanged existing records, and new customer records.
The combined DataFrame should represent only the current customer state.
It should overwrite the existing customer data without storing previous versions.
